newsitem.title: USA: "The Fugitive" case gets DNA tests - newspapers.
newsitem.headline: "The Fugitive" case gets DNA tests - newspapers.

text.p: A third person may have been present at the bludgeoning death more than 40 years ago of the wife of an Ohio osteopath who was the inspiration for "The Fugitive" TV series and movie, it was reported Tuesday.

Dr. Sam Sheppard was convicted in the 1954 killing of his wife Marilyn but acquitted in a new trial in 1966. Until his death in 1970 he maintained a bushy-haired intruder had knocked him unconscious the night of the murder but such an intruder was never found.
The (Akron) Beacon Journal and The (Cleveland) Plain Dealer newspapers reported Tuesday that a DNA expert hired by Sheppard's son found evidence that a third person was at the murder scene.

Marilyn Sheppard, 31 and pregnant, was beaten to death at the couple's suburban Bay Village home July 4, 1954. After a two-month trial that drew heavy press coverage, Sheppard was sentenced to life in prison for second-degree murder.
Unlike the fictional "fugitive" character, Dr. Richard Kimble who claimed a one-armed man was the real killer, Sheppard did not escape from authorities.
He spent 10 years behind bars before a judge freed him in 1964, ruling excessive media coverage tainted the original trial. A second jury acquitted him. He died in 1970 at age 46.

The couple's son, Sam Reese Sheppard, was a 7-year-old boy asleep at home at the time of the murder. He filed a civil lawsuit in 1995 against the state of Ohio, seeking compensation for the decade his father spent in prison.
Indianapolis DNA expert Dr. Mohammed Tahir was assisting in the younger Sheppard's lawsuit, the papers said.

He tested blood samples and other evidence kept from the case as well as a stamp licked by the elder Sheppard in the 1940s and blood taken from a man who was Sheppards' window washer at the time of the murder, the papers said.
